decisions.reason: Across Experiments 1a, 1b, and 2, the authors administer the retrospective gambler's fallacy task (Oppenheimer & Monin, 2009) to new samples as a positive-control replication alongside their replication of Eskine (2013), report the sample sizes, means, SDs, exact difference-in-means, 95% CIs, and standardized effect sizes d in Table 2 and Figure 2, and conclude in the General Discussion that in all cases they observed the expected pattern of results. Only Eskine (2012/2013, row 1078) is in the shipped rows; Oppenheimer & Monin (2009) is a genuine omitted replication target.

corrected_value.title: Enhancing interest and performance with a utility value intervention.

decisions.quote:
The utility value interventions utilized in the current studies

were based on the self-generated utility value interventions

used by Hulleman and colleagues (e.g., Hulleman et al., 2010;
Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009). In addition to replicating this

prior research, we extend it in five ways.
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly frames its classroom utility-value intervention studies (and specifically Study 2 in an undergraduate psychology course) as replicating and extending both Hulleman & Harackiewicz (2009) and Hulleman, Godes, Hendricks, & Harackiewicz (2010, DOI: 10.1037/a0019506), and states in the Study 2 Discussion that Study 2 partially replicated prior research citing both papers. Shipped row 91 covers only Hulleman & Harackiewicz (2009; 10.1126/science.1177067), whereas Hulleman et al. (2010) reports distinct original studies (including Study 2 in an introductory college psychology lecture course) and is absent from the shipped dataset.

corrected_value.title: Why education predicts decreased belief in conspiracy theories.

decisions.quote: Abstract The main aim of the study was to replicate and extend van Prooijen's findings on how education and its outcomes (cognitive complexity, subjective social standing, self‐esteem, a feeling of control and powerlessness, cognitive reflection, epistemic curiosity and scientific reasoning) predict conspiracy beliefs. In two studies (Study 1: N = 497, Mage = 49.06, SDage = 14.92; Study 2: N = 482, Mage = 47.45, SDage = 15.87), subjective socioeconomic status and cognitive reflection (Study 1) and a feeling of powerlessness and scientific reasoning (Study 2) contributed to the negative relationship between education level and belief in conspiracy theories.
decisions.reason: Gligorić et al. (2021) explicitly design Studies 1 (N = 497) and 2 (N = 482) to replicate and extend van Prooijen (2017, Applied Cognitive Psychology, 31(1), 50-58; DOI: 10.1002/acp.3301) on why education predicts decreased belief in conspiracy theories. The only shipped row for this work (row 772) lists Georgiou, Delfabbro, & Balzan (2019), a different cited paper that is not the primary target of the replication, so van Prooijen (2017) is a genuine omitted replication target.

corrected_value.title: Oxytocin facilitates empathic- and self-embarrassment ratings by attenuating amygdala and anterior insula responses.

decisions.quote: The current preregistered pharmacological eye-tracking study employed a randomized within-subject placebo-controlled design to investigate the effects of intranasal OT (24 IU) on patterns of eye gaze in male subjects performing the MET and to replicate previous findings demonstrating OT-induced facilitation of emotional empathy ( Hurlemann et al., 2010 ; Geng et al., 2018a , b ).
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly state in the Introduction and Discussion that their preregistered pharmacological eye-tracking study was designed to replicate previous findings demonstrating oxytocin-induced facilitation of emotional empathy on the multifaceted empathy task (MET), citing Hurlemann et al. (2010) and Geng et al. (2018a, 2018b) together and confirming those findings in the results and discussion. Shipped row 469 captures only Hurlemann et al. (2010), leaving Geng et al. (2018a; Frontiers in Endocrinology, 9:572, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2018.00572) as an omitted replication target.

corrected_value.authors: Geng, Y., Zhao, W., Zhou, F., Ma, X., Yao, S., Hurlemann, R.
corrected_value.title: Oxytocin enhancement of emotional empathy: generalization across cultures and effects on amygdala activity.

decisions.quote: In the current study, we used eye tracking to investigate the effects of intranasal OT on emotional empathy and visual attention to different features of real life pictures in the MET. Results first confirmed previous findings that OT increases emotional empathy in both negative and positive emotional contexts ( Hurlemann et al., 2010 ; Geng et al., 2018a , b ).
decisions.reason: Alongside Hurlemann et al. (2010) and Geng et al. (2018a), the paper explicitly cites Geng et al. (2018b; Frontiers in Neuroscience, 12:512, DOI: 10.3389/fnins.2018.00512) as one of the previous findings of oxytocin-induced facilitation of emotional empathy on the Chinese version of the MET that the present study aimed to replicate and confirmed. Only Hurlemann et al. (2010) is present in shipped row 469, so Geng et al. (2018b) is a genuine omitted replication target.

corrected_value.authors: Schmidt, PJ, Nieman, LK, Danaceau, MA, et al.
corrected_value.title: Differential behavioral effects of gonadal steroids in women with and in those without premenstrual syndrome.

decisions.quote: Here we report a study building on our previous work. We retained our previous sample of 10 women with PMDD and 15 healthy comparison women (cohort 1) and added a second independent cohort of 24 women with PMDD and 61 healthy comparison women (cohort 2). All participants underwent the same ovarian steroid hormone manipulation paradigm. We evaluated differences between cohorts, attempted to replicate our original findings of a differential behavioral sensitivity to otherwise similar changes in ovarian steroids in women with PMDD compared to healthy comparison women (3), and examined several as yet unanswered questions about the effects of ovarian steroids on symptoms in these women.
decisions.reason: This study explicitly adds an independent second cohort (cohort 2: 24 women with PMDD and 61 healthy comparison women) undergoing the same GnRH-agonist (lupron) and estradiol/progesterone addback paradigm to replicate the authors' original findings from cohort 1 reported in reference 3 (Schmidt et al., 1998, New England Journal of Medicine, 338:209-216; DOI: 10.1056/nejm199801223380401). The only shipped row (row 225) is a self-link to this 2017 Translational Psychiatry replication paper itself (10.1038/tp.2017.146), leaving the actual original target Schmidt et al. (1998) omitted.
